title: There’s hope of recovery from COP31 deadlock ‘as long as we learn from it’
summary: The next climate summit that will be held in Ethiopia can be an opportunity to ‘recover lost ambition’

blocks.text: JUSTICE. A member of Fridays for Future holds a placard at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 16, 2026.
The next climate summit that will be held in Ethiopia can be an opportunity to ‘recover lost ambition’
MANILA, Philippines – The failure of talks at the recent UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Turkey is not a new thing — it has happened twice in the past.

Former Philippine lead negotiator Tony La Viña offers a more hopeful stance amid the disappointment surrounding the conclusion of COP31 that failed to build consensus on a cover decision (or what was supposed to be the Antalya Pact).

La Viña recalled the failure of COP6 in The Hague and COP15 in Copenhagen. There was a second COP6 held in Bonn following the failure at The Hague. The COP16 in Cancun was a recovery from the deadlock in Copenhagen — it was where the Green Climate Fund was established.

“I was there both times — as a lead negotiator for the Philippines and developing countries,” La Viña told Rappler in a message. “It was not a big deal — the collapse — as long as we learn lessons from it.” The former negotiator, currently associate director at the Manila Observatory, was present in the summit in Turkey as an observer.

La Viña said he looks forward to the next COP in Ethiopia. “That will be a consequential conference where we cannot afford to fail again; otherwise multilateralism would be considered irrelevant,” he said.
Many countries, climate champions, and civil society groups were disappointed with the outcome of COP31.

According to reports, more than 90 countries rejected the cover decision that failed to mention fossil fuels. Among them are Panama, the Marshall Islands, and the biggest kid on the block, the European Union.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres shared the disappointment felt by many.
“I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But this setback does not change the facts,” he said in a statement.

Local environment groups and Filipino advocates who were present at COP left Turkey just as frustrated as everybody else. Climate activist Joshua Villalobos pointed to the impact to local communities and demanding that polluters “must pay for the solutions.”

The next opportunity for the parties to come together for this high-level talks comes a year from now, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. For Rodne Galicha, climate activist from Sibuyan Island, the sessions leading up to COP32 should “recover lost ambition.”
The credibility of climate negotiations, according to Galicha, rests on how vulnerable communities will benefit from the process. – Rappler.com
